title: Clobetasol Topical: Super-Potent Steroid, Small Surface, Short Course
bottomLine: Clobetasol is a super-potent topical corticosteroid. Safe use means applying a thin layer only to the prescribed site for the prescribed duration and watching for skin atrophy, infection, and systemic steroid effects when large areas, occlusion, or prolonged courses increase absorption.
recognize: Potency, body site, surface area, skin integrity, and occlusion all change absorption.
Face, groin, axillae, and thin skin are especially vulnerable to steroid injury unless specifically directed.
priorities: Verify site, formulation, duration, and whether occlusion is intended.
Escalate marked thinning, striae, worsening infection, or signs of systemic glucocorticoid excess.
assessMonitor: Inspect response, skin integrity, infection, atrophy/telangiectasia, and adherence to duration limits.
interventions: Apply a thin film to affected skin and avoid routine use on uninvolved skin.
medicationSafety: Current 2026 labeling identifies clobetasol as a very high-potency topical corticosteroid; HPA-axis suppression can occur with excessive exposure.
teaching: Use only the prescribed amount/site/duration and wash hands after application unless the hands are being treated.
delegationScope: Routine topical administration may be within PN scope; worsening lesions or suspected systemic effects require licensed-nurse/provider reassessment.
examTrap: Covering clobetasol with an occlusive dressing to make it 'work better' without an order.
oneLinePearl: Super-potent topical steroid = thin layer, small target, short plan.
sourceBasis: DailyMed clobetasol propionate cream labeling updated 2026-05

title: Silver Sulfadiazine: Burn Antimicrobial With Patient-Specific Limits
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Silver sulfadiazine is a topical antimicrobial used in selected burn care. It is not a substitute for burn-depth assessment, debridement/source control, or specialty referral, and exposure can produce sulfonamide-related reactions and transient leukopenia.
recognize: Burn size/depth, age, pregnancy context, allergy history, and wound appearance affect suitability.
Worsening erythema, odor, fever, or systemic instability can indicate invasive infection despite topical therapy.
priorities: Confirm the burn plan and allergy/pregnancy context before application.
Escalate systemic infection, rapidly progressive wound change, or significant blood-count abnormalities.
assessMonitor: Monitor wound progression, infection signs, hypersensitivity, and CBC when clinically indicated for extensive/prolonged exposure.
interventions: Use clean technique and the prescribed wound-care/debridement schedule.
medicationSafety: Current 2026 labeling continues age/pregnancy restrictions and sulfonamide-related precautions.
Topical antimicrobial therapy does not replace burn-center criteria or systemic treatment when invasive infection is suspected.
teaching: Report rash, breathing difficulty, fever, or worsening wound pain/drainage promptly.
delegationScope: Topical burn-medication administration depends on wound-care competency and facility policy; burn progression requires RN/provider reassessment.
examTrap: Treating a deteriorating burn only by applying more topical antimicrobial.
oneLinePearl: Burn cream is adjunct care—the patient and burn depth still drive the plan.
sourceBasis: DailyMed silver sulfadiazine cream labeling updated 2026-07

title: Isotretinoin: Pregnancy Prevention and Whole-Body Toxicity Monitoring
bottomLine: Isotretinoin can be highly effective for severe acne but is profoundly teratogenic and requires iPLEDGE risk-management requirements. Nursing safety also includes mood, liver, lipid, vision, musculoskeletal, and intracranial-hypertension surveillance.
recognize: Pregnancy exposure is the highest-priority preventable harm.
Severe headache with visual symptoms can indicate intracranial hypertension; tetracyclines increase this risk.
priorities: Verify pregnancy-prevention/testing requirements and medication-interaction review.
Escalate pregnancy, severe headache/vision change, major mood change, pancreatitis symptoms, or hepatic injury.
assessMonitor: Trend pregnancy testing where applicable, lipids, hepatic tests, mood/behavior, vision, and adverse effects per regimen.
interventions: Reinforce iPLEDGE steps and avoid blood donation during the restricted interval.
medicationSafety: July 2026 labeling retains the boxed embryo-fetal toxicity warning and iPLEDGE REMS.
Avoid vitamin A duplication and tetracyclines.
teaching: Follow iPLEDGE exactly, do not share medication, and report major mood, vision, or headache changes immediately.
delegationScope: PNs may reinforce ordered education and monitoring; prescribing/REMS eligibility decisions remain authorized prescriber responsibilities.
examTrap: Treating isotretinoin like an ordinary acne drug because the patient feels well.
oneLinePearl: Isotretinoin safety starts with pregnancy prevention and extends far beyond the skin.

title: Topical Tacrolimus: Nonsteroid Eczema Therapy With a Boxed Warning
bottomLine: Topical tacrolimus is a calcineurin inhibitor used for selected atopic dermatitis when steroid-sparing therapy is appropriate. It is for dermatologic use only and current labeling retains a boxed warning about long-term safety, so use should follow indication, age, site, and duration guidance.
recognize: Transient burning/stinging can occur early.
Active skin infection should be assessed rather than masked by immunomodulatory therapy.
priorities: Verify age-appropriate strength, site, and indication.
Escalate persistent lymphadenopathy, severe infection, or unusual/nonhealing lesions.
assessMonitor: Monitor eczema response, infection, lymph nodes when clinically relevant, and ongoing need.
interventions: Apply only to affected skin and avoid ophthalmic/oral exposure.
medicationSafety: April 2026 labeling retains the boxed long-term-safety warning for topical calcineurin inhibitors.
Minimize unnecessary UV exposure as directed by labeling.
teaching: Use the prescribed amount, avoid tanning/UV exposure, and report persistent swollen nodes or nonhealing lesions.
delegationScope: Routine topical administration may be within PN scope; suspected infection or unusual lesions require reassessment.
examTrap: Using topical tacrolimus indefinitely on any rash because it is 'not a steroid.'

title: Dupilumab: Biologic Eczema/Asthma Therapy and Eye-Reaction Surveillance
bottomLine: Dupilumab blocks IL-4/IL-13 signaling and is used across several type-2 inflammatory diseases. Key nursing issues are correct indication, injection technique, ocular reactions, hypersensitivity, and avoiding abrupt replacement of disease-specific rescue therapy.
recognize: Conjunctivitis/keratitis symptoms are especially relevant in atopic-dermatitis patients.
Dupilumab is not an acute rescue medication for asthma attacks.
priorities: Assess indication, current controller/rescue plan, eye symptoms, and hypersensitivity history.
Escalate severe eye pain/vision change, anaphylaxis, or acute respiratory deterioration.
assessMonitor: Monitor disease response, injection reactions, ocular symptoms, and adherence.
interventions: Teach proper subcutaneous technique and storage/handling for the product used.
medicationSafety: Do not stop systemic/topical corticosteroids abruptly solely because dupilumab has started.
teaching: Keep controller/rescue plans intact unless the prescriber changes them and report persistent eye symptoms.
delegationScope: Subcutaneous administration may be within PN scope depending on setting; biologic eligibility and severe adverse-event evaluation require prescriber/RN collaboration.
examTrap: Using dupilumab instead of a rescue bronchodilator during an acute asthma attack.
oneLinePearl: Biologic control is long-term control—not rescue care.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. dupilumab prescribing information reviewed 2026

title: Apremilast: PDE-4 Therapy, GI Effects, Weight, and Mood
bottomLine: Apremilast is an oral PDE-4 inhibitor used for selected psoriasis/psoriatic arthritis and related indications. The main safety decisions are severe GI intolerance/dehydration, weight loss, mood changes, renal dose considerations, and major enzyme-inducer interactions.
recognize: Diarrhea/nausea can be prominent early and may cause volume depletion in vulnerable patients.
Depression or suicidal thinking requires prompt reassessment.
priorities: Review renal function, baseline weight, mood history, and interacting medications.
Escalate severe diarrhea/vomiting, significant weight loss, or suicidal ideation.
assessMonitor: Trend weight, hydration, GI tolerance, mood, and treatment response.
interventions: Support hydration and follow product-specific titration instructions.
medicationSafety: Strong CYP enzyme inducers can reduce exposure and effectiveness.
Dose adjustment is required in severe renal impairment per label.
teaching: Report persistent severe diarrhea, notable weight loss, or mood changes rather than simply stopping follow-up.
delegationScope: Routine administration and symptom monitoring may be within PN scope; renal-dose and psychiatric-risk decisions require prescriber collaboration.
examTrap: Ignoring severe diarrhea in an older adult because it is a 'common' adverse effect.
oneLinePearl: With apremilast, common GI effects become dangerous when hydration, weight, or mood changes.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. apremilast prescribing information reviewed 2026

title: Calcipotriene: Vitamin-D Analog and Calcium-Surface-Area Safety
bottomLine: Calcipotriene is a topical vitamin-D analog used for psoriasis. Safe use means respecting product/site limits and recognizing that excessive exposure can disturb calcium metabolism despite topical administration.
recognize: Irritation is common; severe weakness, confusion, constipation, or polyuria can suggest clinically important hypercalcemia in excessive exposure.
Face and sensitive areas may have product-specific restrictions.
priorities: Verify formulation, site, amount, and concurrent vitamin-D/calcium therapies.
Escalate symptoms concerning for hypercalcemia or severe skin irritation.
assessMonitor: Monitor skin response, irritation, and calcium-related symptoms when exposure is extensive/prolonged.
interventions: Apply only as directed and avoid exceeding product-specific weekly limits.
medicationSafety: Topical vitamin-D analogs are pharmacologically active and can alter calcium with excessive use.
teaching: More medication is not faster psoriasis control; follow the prescribed surface-area and amount limits.
delegationScope: Routine topical administration may be within PN scope; suspected metabolic effects require reassessment.
examTrap: Assuming a topical vitamin-D product cannot affect serum calcium.
oneLinePearl: Topical does not mean biologically inactive—surface area matters.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. calcipotriene prescribing information reviewed 2026

title: Topical Ketoconazole: Fungal Skin Therapy Without Systemic-Azole Assumptions
bottomLine: Topical ketoconazole treats selected superficial fungal/seborrheic conditions. The key exam distinction is that topical therapy has a different systemic-risk profile from oral ketoconazole, while persistent or spreading disease still requires diagnostic reassessment.
recognize: Local burning, irritation, or contact dermatitis can occur.
Failure to improve can mean wrong diagnosis, poor adherence, resistant/atypical infection, or deeper disease.
priorities: Verify the intended site/formulation and avoid eye exposure.
Escalate severe reaction, extensive infection, or treatment failure.
assessMonitor: Monitor rash distribution, pruritus/scale, irritation, and response over the prescribed course.
interventions: Use site-appropriate application technique and complete the directed course.
medicationSafety: Do not transfer oral-ketoconazole hepatotoxicity assumptions directly to topical products, but do not ignore severe local hypersensitivity.
teaching: Avoid eyes/mucosa and continue for the prescribed duration even when symptoms improve early.
delegationScope: Routine topical administration may be within PN scope; failure to improve requires clinician reassessment.
examTrap: Answering an oral-ketoconazole liver-toxicity question when the product is topical shampoo/cream.
oneLinePearl: Always identify the route before applying a drug-class warning.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. topical ketoconazole labeling reviewed 2026

title: Acitretin: Systemic Retinoid With Long Pregnancy Risk
bottomLine: Acitretin is a systemic retinoid for severe psoriasis with major teratogenic, hepatic, lipid, and mucocutaneous risks. Pregnancy prevention extends long after therapy because acitretin can persist/convert to longer-lived metabolites, especially with alcohol exposure.
recognize: Pregnancy prevention is a long-duration safety requirement, not only an on-treatment issue.
Alcohol can promote formation of etretinate and prolong teratogenic risk.
priorities: Verify pregnancy-risk counseling/testing requirements, alcohol avoidance, liver status, lipids, and interacting vitamin-A products.
Escalate pregnancy, severe hepatic symptoms, or major lipid toxicity.
assessMonitor: Trend liver tests, lipids, pregnancy prevention adherence where applicable, and mucocutaneous effects.
interventions: Reinforce strict alcohol avoidance and long-term pregnancy-prevention requirements from the current label.
medicationSafety: Do not combine with vitamin A supplements or other retinoids unless specifically directed.
Blood donation restrictions apply for a prolonged interval.
teaching: Pregnancy risk persists long after the last dose; follow the exact label/prescriber timeline and avoid alcohol.
delegationScope: PNs may reinforce education/monitoring; prescribing and pregnancy-prevention program decisions are prescriber responsibilities.
examTrap: Assuming pregnancy precautions stop when the acitretin prescription ends.
oneLinePearl: Acitretin's teratogenic clock keeps running long after treatment stops.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. acitretin prescribing information reviewed 2026

title: Topical Fluorouracil: Local Destruction, Systemic-Toxicity Red Flags
bottomLine: Topical fluorouracil is used for selected actinic keratoses/superficial lesions and intentionally produces local inflammation. Severe systemic symptoms, unexpected mucosal toxicity, or pregnancy exposure are not expected treatment effects and require escalation.
recognize: Erythema, crusting, and local inflammation can be expected at treated sites.
Profound diarrhea, mucositis, fever, or systemic illness raises concern for excessive absorption or unusual susceptibility such as DPD deficiency.
priorities: Verify exact lesion/site and application boundaries.
Escalate severe systemic toxicity, pregnancy, or rapidly worsening infection at the site.
assessMonitor: Monitor local reaction severity, healing, adherence, and systemic symptoms.
interventions: Use gloves/applicator as directed and avoid unintended skin/mucosal contact.
medicationSafety: Do not confuse topical fluorouracil with systemic chemotherapy dosing/administration.
teaching: Expected local inflammation should stay localized; report severe whole-body symptoms promptly.
delegationScope: Topical administration may be within PN scope; lesion diagnosis and severe toxicity evaluation require clinician oversight.
examTrap: Stopping at the first expected redness without distinguishing therapeutic local inflammation from dangerous systemic toxicity.
oneLinePearl: Topical 5-FU should look locally active—not make the patient systemically ill.
sourceBasis: Current U.S. topical fluorouracil prescribing information reviewed 2026
